parole.significato: August (the eighth month of the Roman, Julian, and Gregorian calendars, following July and preceding September)
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic аугоустъ (augustŭ), авъгоустъ (avŭgustŭ), from Ancient Greek Αὔγουστος (Aúgoustos), in turn from Latin Augustus, named after the emperor Caesar Augustus.
From Old Church Slavonic агарѣнинъ (agarěninŭ), from Ancient Greek ἀγαρηνός (agarēnós), derived from Hagar, canonically the mother of Ishmael in the Bible.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic адъ (adŭ), from Ancient Greek ᾍδης (Hāídēs).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic азъбоукꙑ (azŭbuky), from the names of the first two letters of the Cyrillic alphabet, азъ (azŭ) + боукꙑ (buky), a calque of Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic амъвонъ (amŭvonŭ), from Ancient Greek ἄμβων (ámbōn).
From Old Church Slavonic амин (amin) аминь (aminĭ), аминъ (aminŭ), from Ancient Greek ᾱ̓μήν (āmḗn), from Biblical Hebrew אָמֵן (“certainly, verily”).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic ангелъ (angelŭ), from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos).
From Old Church Slavonic благословити (blagosloviti), itself a calque of Ancient Greek ἐυλογέω (eulogéō).
From Old Church Slavonic благословити (blagosloviti), itself a calque of Ancient Greek εὐλογέω (eulogéō).

parole.significato: pious, devout (living according to Christian morals)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic благочьстивъ (blagočĭstivŭ), a calque of Ancient Greek εὐσεβής (eusebḗs). By surface analysis, бла́го (blágo) + чест (čest) + -ив (-iv).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic благочьстьѥ (blagočĭstĭje), a calque of Ancient Greek εὐσέβεια (eusébeia). By surface analysis, благо- (blago-) + чест (čest) + -ие (-ie).

parole.significato: long-suffering, forbearance (merciful and patient endurance, especially as a Christian virtue or divine quality)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic длъготрьпѣниѥ (dlŭgotrĭpěnije), Calque of Ancient Greek μακροθυμία (makrothumía). By surface analysis, дълъг (dălăg) + -о- (-o-) + търпе́ние (tărpénie).
From Old Church Slavonic диꙗволъ (dijavolŭ), диꙗволь (dijavolĭ), borrowed from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos, “accuser, slanderer”).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic єпархиꙗ (eparxija), derived from Ancient Greek ἐπαρχία (eparkhía).

parole.significato: idol (an object of worship, often embodying a deity)
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic идоль (idolĭ), ultimately from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”). Other cognates include Albanian idhull, Romanian idol, English idol, etc.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic инокъ (inokŭ), itself a calque of Ancient Greek μοναχός (monakhós). By surface analysis, ин (in, “one, separated, alone”) + -ок (-ok).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic маслина (maslina), itself a calque of Ancient Greek ἐλαίᾱ (elaíā). By surface analysis, масло́ (masló) + -ина (-ina).
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic монахъ (monaxŭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мъстъ (mŭstŭ), borrowed from Ancient Greek μοῦστος (moûstos).

parole.significato: organ, pipe organ (a large, complex keyboard wind instrument in which sound is produced by air driven through metallic…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic оръганъ (orŭganŭ), borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄργᾰνον (órgănon).
From Old Church Slavonic попъ (popŭ), from Ancient Greek πάπας (pápas), variant of πάππας (páppas, “daddy, papa”). Doublet of па́па (pápa).

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic сандалии f (sandalii), itself derived from Ancient Greek σάνδαλον (sándalon, “sandal”). The masculine has spread at a more recent time, probably under the influence of Western languages.
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic сѵнаго́га (sünagóga), from Ancient Greek σῠνᾰγωγή (sŭnăgōgḗ, “assembly, gathering”).

From Old Church Slavonic скрапии m (skrapii), скрапиꙗ f (skrapija) (reflecting Proto-Slavic *skorpьjь, *skorpьja), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek σκορπῐ́ος (skorpĭ́os), interpreted as a derivative with the suffix -ей (-ej). Inherited from Old Church Slavonic тръжьство (trŭžĭstvo), a semantic loan of Ancient Greek πᾰνήγῠρῐς (pănḗgŭrĭs); thus, by this connection, related to Ancient Greek ᾰ̓γορᾱ́ (ăgorā́) and its relatives. Inherited from Old Church Slavonic оусъпенѥ (usŭpenje). Calque of Ancient Greek κοίμησις (τῆς Θεοτόκου) (koímēsis (tês Theotókou), “Dormition (of the Mother of God)”).

Inherited from Old Church Slavonic фараѡнъ (faraonŭ), borrowed from Ancient Greek Φαραώ (Pharaṓ), borrowed from Biblical Hebrew פַּרְעֹה, borrowed from Egyptian pr-ꜥꜣ (“palace, pharaoh”, literally “pr (“house”) + ꜥꜣ (“great, big”)”).

parole.significato: soundness of mind and soul, prudence, chastity
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic цѣломѫдрьѥ (cělomǫdrĭje), а Calque of Ancient Greek σωφροσύνη (sōphrosúnē). Formed as цял (cjal, “whole”) + -о- (-o-) + мъ́дър (mắdăr, “wise”) + -ие (-ie).

parole.significato: wonderworker, thaumaturge - one who performs miracles (epithet of a saint)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic чоудотворьць (čudotvorĭcĭ), itself a calque of Ancient Greek θαυματουργός (thaumatourgós). By surface analysis, чу́до (čúdo) + -о- (-o-) + творе́ц (tvoréc). Compare Russian чудотворец (čudotvorec) and Serbo-Croatian чудотворац.
From Old Church Slavonic школа (škola), ultimately from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).
